[LangGraph](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/) is a library for building stateful, multi-actor applications with LLMs, and is often used to build agent and multi-agent workflows. body:
Awesome start - thanks for leading on this! Reading over this as a user, here are my thoughts:

Structure:

Right now it feels like we could focus / frame the narrative more around user needs.

Maybe instead of just tool node -> execute manually -> non-explicit tools, we could frame it based on what the user wants to accomplish. These approaches aren’t mutually exclusive but illustrate ways we use tool calling to accomplish different tasks.

1. ToolNode: Directly execute tool functions.
    1. When it’s useful: if you can define utilities in specific 
    2.  Routing is between two nodes (llm and tool node). End condition is if no tool calls are present. Always execute values in the tool calls of the last ai message.
2. Customize the tool node: 
    1. Routing can still be between two nodes (llm and tool node). End condition is if no tool calls are present.
    2. Can combine the LLM’s provided values with other state or custom variables. Or could stream nested inputs within a node, etc.
3. Customize Routing: 
    1. “Tools” don’t have to be single functions, they are just ways for an LLM to generate structured output that your application can use. How it uses it is up to you. Some tools may not even correspond with a single scoped “tool” - they can be used for routing or for responding in a structured format. 
    2. We could actually maybe provide two examples here:
        1. If you want your app to “remember” the previous actions it has taken: maintain the `messages` list: The agent / llm node is the same as above and returns  messages
        2. If you want complete control and don’t want your LLM to keep track of all the previous action turns as messages: The llm uses `with_structured_output` or something similar and we store that schema in the state rather than as a message

And then remind the user again that these aren’t exhaustive or mutually exclusive.




Finally,  my take on general /style points for the final draft:

- Remove unnecessary adjectives (“simple”) and adverbs (“very”, “extremely” )  - either be specific about what the user gains or what something does, or remove entirely if it’s not meant to communicate something specific.
- For built-ins like “ToolNode”, link to the reference doc (https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/reference/prebuilt/#toolnode)
- Try to avoid “lots of”  - this is intimidating to a reader. The reader needs it cleanly spelled out based on the distinct jobs they do. If there are two ways of doing something, just show one, or motivate the second example with a real need “I need to be able to combine the LLM output with other variables and so will choose to customize how I execute the tool calling a node”

body:
Ya. This seems clever. 

1/ We want the agent to explicitly call a `grade documents` tool. 
2/ But, we don't want the tool arguments to include the raw documents. This has high token cost.
3/ So, the tool call simply asks the LLM to show its work with `step_by_step_reasoning` and provide the grade, `score`.
4/ We then use this to route to the next tool.
so you simply have the LLM compress its grading into the tool call itself.

I'd also add that it's important to manage the reader's expectations throughout. Don't bury the lede. Avoid surprise when running code. Use words like "Next we can run X & Y. We will expect Z.". body:
Can add some text -- 

By default, `StateGraph` takes in a single schema and all nodes are expected to communicate with that schema. However, it is also possible to [define explicit input and output schemas for a graph](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/how-tos/input_output_schema/?h=input+outp).

Often, in these cases, we define an "internal" schema that contains *all* keys relevant to graph operations. But, we use specific `input` and `output` schemas to filter what's permitted when invoking and what's returned. We use type hints below to, for example, show that the output of `answer_node` will be filtered to `OutputState`. In addition, we define each node's input schema (e.g., as `state: OverallState` for `answer_node`).

body:
> Sometimes we need to pass values to our tools at runtime. For example, you might want to give tools access to:

I think language like this may contribute to people thinking you "have to" use langchain, etc. 

I don't have a perfect ording but all this is more like:

"Tools" are functions you've exposed to the model. Sometimes, you want to let the LLM populate only a subset of the functions' arguments; your program can provide the rest. If you're using LangChain-style tools, an easy way to handle this is by annotating function parameters with `InjectedArg`. This excludes that parameter from being shown to the LLM.

If you're using LangGraph's prebuilt ToolNode, we have a couple additional special `InejectedArg` types you can use to tell the graph to populate the tool with values from the state, store, or configuration.

body:
```suggestion
Instead of hard-coding a fixed control flow, we sometimes want LLM systems that can pick their own control flow to solve more complex problems! This is one definition of an [agent](https://blog.langchain.dev/what-is-an-agent/): *an agent is a system that uses an LLM to decide the control flow of an application.* There are many ways that an LLM can control application:
```
author: vbarda

body:
```suggestion
Many LLM applications implement a particular control flow of steps before and / or after LLM calls. As an example, [RAG](https://github.com/langchain-ai/rag-from-scratch) performs retrieval of documents relevant to a user question, and passes those documents to an LLM in order to ground the model's response in the provided document context. 
```
author: vbarda

body:
```suggestion
A router allows an LLM to select a single step from a specified set of options. This is an agent architecture that exhibits a relatively limited level of control because the LLM usually focuses on making a single decision and produces a specific output from limited set of pre-defined options. Routers typically employ a few different concepts to achieve this.
```
author: vbarda

body:
```suggestion
1. Prompt engineering: Instructing the LLM to respond in a specific format via the system prompt.
```
author: vbarda

body:
```suggestion
2. Output parsers: Using post-processing to extract structured data from LLM responses.
```
author: vbarda

body:
```suggestion
Tools are useful whenever you want an agent to interact with external systems. External systems (e.g., APIs) often require a particular input schema or payload, rather than natural language. When we bind an API, for example, as a tool, we give the model awareness of the required input schema. The model will choose to call a tool based upon the natural language input from the user and it will return an output that adheres to the tool's required schema. 
```
author: vbarda

body:
```suggestion
In the ReAct architecture, an LLM is called repeatedly in a while-loop. At each step the agent decides which tools to call, and what the inputs to those tools should be. Those tools are then executed, and the outputs are fed back into the LLM as observations. The while-loop terminates when the agent decides it has enough information to solve the user request and it is not worth calling any more tools.
```
author: vbarda

body:
```suggestion
As a result, there are many different types of [agent architectures](https://blog.langchain.dev/what-is-a-cognitive-architecture/), which give an LLM varying levels of control. 
```

This loop is creating ToolNodes, and if you have multiple ToolNodes, you likely want `ignore_unknown_tool_calls=True`.

ToolNode as its implemented now is assuming that each `"messages"` key is handled by one ToolNode (I think). ## RADAR Review

**Score:** 7/10

| Severity   | Count |
|------------|-------|
| Critical   | 0     |
| Warning    | 2     |
| Suggestion | 2     |
| Praise     | 1     |

---

Score: 7/10 — The PR cleanly adds string-based embed specification with good error messaging and lazy import handling. The main concerns are: (1) `lru_cache` on the import-probe function permanently caches a `None` result, which can cause subtle failures in test environments and is hard to reset; (2) the version detection in the error path doesn't actually verify that the installed langchain version has `init_embeddings`, so the error message can be misleading; (3) the return value from `init_embeddings` is not validated as an `Embeddings` instance. The docstring has a minor inconsistency ("three ways" vs four). Overall the feature is well-scoped and the implementation is straightforward, but the caching strategy and error-path accuracy deserve attention before shipping.

body:
My preference for ordering components, loosely base on importance and the probable order in which the user will actually interact with each component.
```
LangGraph Server (most important, it's the main thing)
LangGraph CLI (user uses the CLI to launch the server)
LangGraph Studio (user uses the Studio to interact with the server and test code changes)
LangGraph SDK (user writes client code to call the server)
LangGraph Data Plane (all the components of a deployed server, only relevant for deployment though)
LangGraph Control Plane
```

client side code looks like this:

dynamic:

author: pedro-inf-custodio

body:
```suggestion
@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_astream_usage_metadata_preserved():
    class MessagesState(TypedDict):
        messages: Annotated[list[AnyMessage], add_messages]

    usage_metadata = {"input_tokens": 10, "output_tokens": 5, "total_tokens": 15}
    ai_msg = AIMessage(content="Test", id="1", usage_metadata=usage_metadata)
    human_msg = HumanMessage(content="Hello", id="2")

    def chat(_: MessagesState) -> MessagesState:
        return {"messages": [human_msg, ai_msg]}

    builder = StateGraph(MessagesState)
    builder.add_node(chat)
    builder.add_edge(START, "chat")
    graph = builder.compile()

    found = False
    async for chunk in graph.astream_events({"messages": []}, stream_mode="messages"):
        event = chunk.get("event")
        if event == "on_chain_stream":
            msg = chunk.get("data", {}).get("chunk", {})
            if not msg or not isinstance(msg, tuple):
                continue

            message, _ = msg
            if getattr(message, "id", None) == "1":
                additional_kwargs = getattr(message, "additional_kwargs", {})
                assert "usage_metadata" in additional_kwargs, (
                    f"usage_metadata missing in additional_kwargs: {additional_kwargs}"
                )
                assert additional_kwargs["usage_metadata"] == usage_metadata
                found = True
    assert found, "Did not find AIMessage with usage_metadata in astream_events"
```

@eyurtsev 

  Thank you for the feedback! I understand that CI should rely on the Makefile's lint definition.

  However, there's a challenge with Windows runners: they don't have `make` available by default. So I'd like to discuss implementation policy. I am thinking of using OS specific conditions, what do you think?
  - Ubuntu: runs `make test`
  - Windows: runs the underlying commands directly

  For the lint workflow, I'm thinking of following the same pattern:
  ```yaml
  - name: Run lint (Unix)
    if: steps.changed-files.outputs.all && matrix.os == 'ubuntu-latest'
    working-directory: ${{ inputs.working-directory }}
    run: make lint

  - name: Run lint (Windows)
    if: steps.changed-files.outputs.all && matrix.os == 'windows-latest'
    working-directory: ${{ inputs.working-directory }}
    shell: bash
    run: |
      # Mirror the Makefile lint target for Windows
      uv run ruff check .
      uv run ruff format langgraph --diff
      uv run ruff check --select I langgraph
      mkdir -p .mypy_cache
      uv run mypy langgraph --cache-dir .mypy_cache
  ```

  This approach maintains consistency with the existing CI patterns while ensuring Windows compatibility. Would this be acceptable, or do you
  have a different preference for handling Windows environments?

```suggestion
In this example, no reducer function is supplied which means the old value will be replaced with the new value when a state update is made. Let's assume the input to the graph is `{ foo: 1, bar: ["hi"] }`. Let's then assume the first `Node` returns `{ foo: 2 }`. This is treated as an update to the state. Notice that the `Node` does not need to return the whole `State` schema - just an update. After applying this update, the `State` would then be `{ foo: 2, bar: ["hi"] }`. If the second node returns `{ bar: ["bye"] }` then the `State` would then be `{ foo: 2, bar: ["bye"] }`
```

body:
## Pull Request Overview

This PR adds support for tools to clear the entire message history by allowing `Command` updates to contain only a `RemoveMessage(id=REMOVE_ALL_MESSAGES)` without triggering validation errors. Previously, the `ToolNode` validation required a matching `ToolMessage` for every tool call, which prevented tools from clearing all messages as this special case doesn't require a `ToolMessage`.

- Modified validation logic in `_validate_tool_command` to bypass `ToolMessage` validation when removing all messages
- Added comprehensive test coverage for the new functionality
- Enhanced error handling to support message history clearing use cases

### Reviewed Changes

Copilot reviewed 2 out of 2 changed files in this pull request and generated 2 comments.

| File | Description |
| ---- | ----------- |
| libs/prebuilt/langgraph/prebuilt/tool_node.py | Added logic to detect and allow `RemoveMessage(id=REMOVE_ALL_MESSAGES)` as sole message update, bypassing ToolMessage validation |
| libs/prebuilt/tests/test_tool_node.py | Added test case verifying tools can return Command with RemoveMessage to clear all messages without validation errors |

body:
**Security Issues**
- SQL Injection via string interpolation in LIMIT clause
The alist method constructs the SQL query using an f-string for the LIMIT value: `query += f\" LIMIT {limit}\"`. This violates the project's SQL guardrails requiring parameterized queries and allows an attacker controlling `limit` to inject SQL.  

Recommendations
- Use a parameterized placeholder for LIMIT and append the limit value to the args tuple: `query += \" LIMIT %s\"` and `args = (*args, limit)`.
- Alternatively, enforce strict integer casting/validation before using the value and still prefer parameterized queries to comply with guardrails.
author: corridor-security

body:
The `limit` value is concatenated directly into the SQL string, violating the project's guardrails and enabling SQL injection if `limit` is user-controlled.

```python
if limit:
    query += f" LIMIT {limit}"
```

Use a parameterized placeholder and pass `limit` as a separate argument to `execute()`.

Example remediation:
- Change to a placeholder and append to args: `query += " LIMIT %s"` and `args = (*args, limit)`
- Ensure `limit` is an integer before binding.

This ensures compliance with the SQL guardrails (parameterized queries, no f-strings with user input) and prevents injection via the LIMIT clause.

For more details, see the [finding in Corridor](https://app.corridor.dev/projects/310af3f2-00f7-413d-8311-2265c3518990/findings/3eec6f98-ea9d-44e4-b10b-6c14f2f5c175).

**Provide feedback**: Reply with whether this is a valid vulnerability or false positive to help improve Corridor's accuracy.

to not change the current api:
```python
result1 = graph.invoke(...)

# len(result1.get(__interrupt__, []) == 2)

result2 = graph.invoke(Command(resume=interrupt_1_resume_map) 
# interrupt_2 task is skipped because no resume value provided
# we still should output writes for this blocked task so it is visible in the result:
# len(result2.get(__interrupt__, []) == 1) #interrupt_2  <-- only appears because we call output_writes for this blocked task

result3 = graph.invoke(Command(resume=interrupt_2_resume_map) 
# len(result2.get(__interrupt__, []) == 0)
```

body:
What happened before is:
1. We would prepare the PUSH task (a Send to the node that contains the interrupt). 
2. The runner would execute this task and that node would re-execute, and we would encounter the interrupt again. 3. Since there is no resume value for this interrupt, we re-raise. 

Raising the interrupt here short-circuits this process; we prevent 2. from happening unecessarily

I'll clarify this in a comment

body:
```
# super-step 0:
1. __start__ -> node_a
2. node_a writes ["a"]

# super-step 1:
3. node_a -> node_b
4. node_b writes ["b"]
5. node_a -> node_c
6. node_c overwrites with ["c"]
```
Given this order, before 6 happens, the binop channel holds ["a", "b"]. So when we overwrite with ["c"], it just sets the channel val to ["c"]
Also note that [3, 4] can be swapped with [5, 6] (node_c can overwrite before its paralle node node_b writes) and the result will be the same, because the flag `seen_overwrite` is set to `True` for the super-step once an overwrite is encountered

body:
In 3.14, `__annotations__` is no longer a simple class attribute but a descriptor. But this is not specific to Pydantic, every Python class behaves like this.

More importantly, it's no longer safe to directly access `your_cls.__annotations__`, as this will trigger the evaluation logic and raise a `NameError` if some annotations are still deferred and not resolvable yet.

You will find extensive documentation about this in:
- https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/annotationlib.html
- https://docs.python.org/3.14/howto/annotations.html#annotations-howto

What you seem to want to achieve here is to only fetch the annotations keys, without caring about the values. Right now your change will just silently ignore all annotations under 3.14 which is probably not what you want. You can work around this by using [`annotationlib.get_annotations(obj, format=Format.FORWARDREF)`](https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/annotationlib.html#annotationlib.get_annotations) and grabbing the keys from there.

body:
**Security Issues**
- SQL Injection due to string interpolation of LIMIT in alist()
In alist(), the LIMIT clause is constructed via an f-string: `query += f" LIMIT {limit}"`. This violates the project guardrail to use driver-native placeholders and avoid f-strings with user-supplied data. If an attacker can influence the `limit` parameter (e.g., via an API layer calling this library), they could inject arbitrary SQL (e.g., `"0; DROP TABLE checkpoints;--"`). Use a parameterized placeholder for LIMIT and pass `limit` as an additional argument to `fetch()`, and/or strictly validate `limit` is an integer before use.
author: corridor-security

body:
The LIMIT clause is built using direct string interpolation, which enables SQL injection if `limit` is attacker-controlled:

```python
query = SELECT_SQL + where + " ORDER BY checkpoint_id DESC"
if limit:
    query += f" LIMIT {limit}"
```

This violates the repository's SQL guardrails (no f-strings with user data). An attacker could supply a malicious value (e.g., `"0; DROP TABLE checkpoints;--"`) leading to destructive queries.

Remediation:
- Use a parameterized placeholder for LIMIT and append the value to the argument list instead of interpolating it. For example:
  - Compute the next positional placeholder index (e.g., `placeholder = len(args) + 1`) and do `query += f" LIMIT ${placeholder}"` then `args.append(int(limit))`.
- Additionally, coerce/validate `limit` to an integer (e.g., `limit = int(limit)` and ensure non-negative bounds) before using it.
- Do not construct SQL clauses with f-strings or string concatenation using any user-influenced input.


For more details, see the [finding in Corridor](https://app.corridor.dev/projects/310af3f2-00f7-413d-8311-2265c3518990/findings/a11f61ee-365a-4d4d-8ea0-41408517315a).

**Provide feedback**: Reply with whether this is a valid vulnerability or false positive to help improve Corridor's accuracy.

Great call outs. Honestly, we don't need to differentiate between the tenant ID and key ID as the value for both will be the same in our case.

We already integrated with the Auth decorator, and we provided a custom JWT header, that we decrypt/decode and extract multiple claims. One of the claims that we passed inside the JWT payload (as a header), is the tenant ID (aka brand ID) and that is the only key that we need to pass to our encryption decryption layer (along  with the data that needs to be encrypted/decrypted.
author: jorgeg-qualtrics

body:
Something like this:

```
@auth.authenticate
async def authenticate(request: Request) -> Auth.types.MinimalUserDict:
    if request.url.path in NO_AUTH_PATHS:
        return None
    passed_token = request.headers.get("x-jwt", None)
    if passed_token is None:
        raise Auth.exceptions.HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Missing X-JWT Header")

.... <redacted code> ....

    result.update({
        "identity": identity,
        "display_name": user_id,
        "is_authenticated": True,
        "permissions": [],

        # Qualtrics specific dictionary elements (key and values)
        "issuer": issuer,
        "brandId": brand_id,
        "userId": user_id,
        "identityOverride": identity_override,
        "used_auth_token": used_auth_token
    })
    return result
```

This allows us to later own retrieve the tenant ID which is also our desired key ID as `ctx.user["brandId"]` or `ctx.user.brandId`
author: jorgeg-qualtrics

body: We prefer extracting this from the JWT claims (provided as a X-JWT Header) and obtained in the Auth layer/middleware, as it adds extra security because the claims/ jwt-payload is encrypted at transit and trusted that it was not tampered with
author: jorgeg-qualtrics

body:
This is a great idea, because we will need to be able to preserve ownership enforement and searching capabilities:

not all data is necessarily encrypted at rest. Certain data (e.g. Qualtrics-defined data), such as brand IDs or internal keys may not be encrypted, both because it’s not customer data and it may be necessary to facilitate internal operations (e.g. logging, data cleanup, etc…).
author: jorgeg-qualtrics

body: This client always provides the same value for the encryption context header. In practice, we need to dynamically pass different tenant IDs/key IDs (in our case it is the same) per request. We already created our own SDK clients that provide a dynamic JWT header per request which injects different values for the brand ID (aka tenant ID). This is because we invoke the same graph for different tenants and need to reuse the client in a way that each API can receive different values for those headers (instead of being always the same during initialization)
author: jorgeg-qualtrics

body: This makes the encryption isolated from Auth and ownership (authN&authZ). Ideally, we would like to tie the encryption to the auth layers, so we can also trust that the client asking for decrypted data is also the owner of such data/resources

## Pull request overview This PR hardens the checkpoint-sqlite library against SQL injection attacks by converting manual string escaping to parameterized queries and implementing comprehensive security tests. The changes ensure all user input (filter keys and values, LIMIT parameters) is safely handled through proper validation and parameterized queries. **Key changes:** - Replaces manual string escaping (`value.replace("'", "''")`) with parameterized queries (`?` placeholders) for all filter values - Implements `_validate_filter_key()` to prevent SQL injection through malicious filter keys - Fixes LIMIT clause to use parameterized queries and handle `limit=0` correctly with `if limit is not None` - Adds comprehensive security tests for SQL injection prevention, numeric edge cases (NaN, infinity), and special characters ### Reviewed changes Copilot reviewed 7 out of 7 changed files in this pull request and generated 2 comments.
Show a summary per file | File | Description | | ---- | ----------- | | `libs/checkpoint-sqlite/langgraph/store/sqlite/base.py` | Converts all filter value handling to parameterized queries; adds pre-compiled regex pattern for filter key validation; improves type annotation formatting | | `libs/checkpoint-sqlite/langgraph/checkpoint/sqlite/utils.py` | Adds `_validate_filter_key()` function and pre-compiled regex pattern; integrates validation into `_metadata_predicate()` | | `libs/checkpoint-sqlite/langgraph/checkpoint/sqlite/__init__.py` | Updates LIMIT clause to use parameterized query and fixes condition to `if limit is not None` | | `libs/checkpoint-sqlite/langgraph/checkpoint/sqlite/aio.py` | Updates async LIMIT clause to use parameterized query and fixes condition to `if limit is not None` | | `libs/checkpoint-sqlite/tests/test_store.py` | Adds comprehensive security tests: SQL injection prevention (filter keys and values), numeric edge cases (NaN, infinity, large numbers), boolean filters, and keys with hyphens/digits | | `libs/checkpoint-sqlite/tests/test_sqlite.py` | Adds security tests for checkpoint metadata filters: SQL injection prevention, LIMIT parameter safety, and keys with hyphens/digits | | `libs/checkpoint-sqlite/tests/test_aiosqlite.py` | Implements limit/before parameter tests (replacing TODO); adds SQL injection prevention test for async LIMIT parameter | **⚠️ Critical Issue:** The tests `test_filter_keys_with_hyphens_and_digits` and `test_metadata_filter_keys_with_hyphens_and_digits` will fail because they expect keys like `access-level` and `123abc` to work, but the production code builds invalid JSON paths (`$.access-level` instead of `$["access-level"]`). body:
**Critical: Tests will fail due to invalid JSON path construction**

The tests `test_filter_keys_with_hyphens_and_digits` (line 1176) and `test_metadata_filter_keys_with_hyphens_and_digits` (line 274 in test_sqlite.py) expect keys with hyphens or starting with digits to work, but the current implementation builds JSON paths like `$.access-level` or `$.123abc` which are invalid SQLite JSON1 syntax.

The test docstrings acknowledge this: "Current unquoted JSON path construction...is not valid JSON1 syntax" and "This exposes incorrect JSON path handling (unquoted segments)."

**These tests will fail when run** because:
1. Keys containing hyphens (like `access-level`) cannot be accessed with `$.access-level`
2. Keys starting with digits (like `123abc`) cannot be accessed with `$.123abc`
3. SQLite JSON1 requires bracket notation: `$["access-level"]` and `$["123abc"]`

**Options:**
1. Mark these tests with `@pytest.mark.xfail` to document known failures
2. Fix the JSON path construction in production code to make the tests pass
3. Remove the tests until the implementation is ready

The production code needs a helper function to properly quote JSON path segments that contain hyphens or start with digits, affecting all JSON path construction in:
- `libs/checkpoint-sqlite/langgraph/store/sqlite/base.py` (lines 410-434, 641-702, 861-922)
- `libs/checkpoint-sqlite/langgraph/checkpoint/sqlite/utils.py` (line 69)

body:
**Security Issues**
- Information Exposure Through Error Messages
  `A2AProtocolHandler` exposes raw Python exception messages — including file paths, module names, and internal state hints — to peer agents via `A2AResponse.create_error(error_message=str(e))`. This pattern appears in all three execution paths: `handle_request` (sync), `ahandle_request` (async), and `stream_request` (streaming). While no HTTP server route is wired up in this PR, the A2A spec explicitly treats callers as potentially untrusted peers, and the `disable_a2a` CLI flag signals that these handlers are intended to be exposed over the network in a future (or separate) server layer. Returning `str(e)` violates guardrail 44 and CWE-209; all three sites should replace `str(e)` with a generic message and log the full exception server-side.
author: corridor-security

body:
Returning raw exception messages to the requester exposes internal details (file paths, configuration hints) to untrusted peers. This can be triggered by crafted inputs and violates guardrail 44 (do not expose raw exception details).

```python
except Exception as e:
    return A2AResponse.create_error(
        task_id=request.task_id,
        error_message=str(e),
        error_code="EXECUTION_ERROR",
        responder_agent_id=self.agent_id,
    )
```

Remediation: Return a generic error message to clients and log the detailed exception server-side.

```suggestion
                error_message="Internal error",
```

For more details, see the [finding in Corridor](https://app.corridor.dev/projects/310af3f2-00f7-413d-8311-2265c3518990/findings/41bcb730-71ae-4a98-89b3-1c641b41905d).

**Provide feedback**: Reply with whether this is a valid vulnerability or false positive to help improve Corridor's accuracy.

body:
## Summary

This PR successfully adds Pyodide/WASM support to LangGraph by making C extensions optional. The implementation approach is sound:

**Strengths:**
- Excellent fallback strategy for `ormsgpack` using `msgpack` with a well-designed compatibility layer
- Smart use of optional dependencies (`fast` extras) to maintain performance on native Python
- Clean try-except pattern for handling import failures
- Good documentation in docstrings

**Required Changes:**
- The MD5 hash fallback is causing CI/CD security checks to fail. Replace MD5 with SHA-256 in both `libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_algo.py` and `libs/langgraph/langgraph/types.py`

**Recommendations:**
- Consider adding tests for the ormsgpack compatibility layer to ensure edge cases work correctly in WASM environments

Once the MD5 issue is resolved, this will be ready to merge.
author: aaron-seq

body:
The CodeQL security check is failing because MD5 is flagged as a weak cryptographic hashing algorithm. While using `usedforsecurity=False` is correct for non-cryptographic purposes, it's not sufficient to pass the security check.

As Copilot Autofix suggests, replacing MD5 with SHA-256 would resolve the security alert:

```python
def xxh3_128_hexdigest(data: bytes) -> str:
    """Fallback using SHA-256 for environments without xxhash (e.g., Pyodide/WASM)."""
    return hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()
```

This change maintains the same function signature while using a more secure hashing algorithm. The same fix should be applied to both occurrences in `libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_algo.py` (line 40) and `libs/langgraph/langgraph/types.py` (line 30).
author: aaron-seq

body: Great approach! Making these C extensions optional with a `fast` extra is the right way to maintain WASM compatibility while still allowing users to install the faster C-based packages on native Python. This follows the same pattern as other libraries and provides a clear upgrade path for users who want better performance.
author: aaron-seq

body:
Excellent implementation of the compatibility layer! The `_OrmsgpackCompat` class effectively mimics the ormsgpack API using msgpack as a fallback. The `_pairs_hook` function is particularly clever for handling list-to-tuple conversion during dict construction, which is necessary for hashable keys.

One minor suggestion: Consider adding a test to ensure the compatibility layer properly handles edge cases like nested data structures with list keys, to verify that the fallback behavior matches ormsgpack's behavior in WASM environments.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Align latest checkpoint ordering with list() semantics**

`get_tuple()` now picks the last inserted checkpoint via `next(reversed(checkpoints))`, but `list()` in the same module still orders checkpoints by `checkpoint_id` (`sorted(..., key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True)`). body: ## Pull request overview This pull request fixes incorrect `Command.PARENT` bubbling behavior when checkpoint namespaces include numeric task-disambiguation segments (e.g., `|1`). The runtime can insert purely numeric segments between `name:task_id` segments in nested/fanout scenarios (e.g., `parent_first:|1|node:`). The previous logic only removed numeric segments at the end of the namespace, which could produce malformed parent graph identifiers and prevent commands from routing correctly. **Changes:** - Updated namespace filtering logic in both sync (`run_with_retry`) and async (`arun_with_retry`) retry paths to filter out ALL numeric segments, not just trailing ones - Added comprehensive documentation explaining the checkpoint namespace structure and why numeric segments need to be filtered - Added regression tests for nested invocation scenarios to verify `Command.PARENT` correctly routes to the parent graph ### Reviewed changes Copilot reviewed 3 out of 3 changed files in this pull request and generated 3 comments. | File | Description | | ---- | ----------- | | libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_retry.py | Updated namespace filtering logic in both sync and async retry handlers to drop all numeric segments before computing parent namespace, with detailed inline documentation | | libs/langgraph/tests/test_parent_command.py | Added sync regression test that exercises nested invocations with Command.PARENT to verify correct routing | | libs/langgraph/tests/test_parent_command_async.py | Added test file for async scenarios (though currently uses sync execution) | --- 💡 Add Copilot custom instructions for smarter, more guided reviews. body:
The logic to filter out numeric segments from the checkpoint namespace duplicates the functionality of the existing `recast_checkpoint_ns` function from `langgraph._internal._config`. Consider using that function instead of reimplementing the same logic. While `recast_checkpoint_ns` also strips task IDs (by splitting on NS_END), this should not affect the correctness of the parent namespace computation since we only need to drop numeric segments and then get the parent by removing the last segment.

However, note that `recast_checkpoint_ns` performs `part.split(NS_END)[0]` which would strip task IDs, and here we might want to preserve them. If task ID preservation is important for the parent_ns, then the current implementation is correct and this is not an issue. Please verify whether task IDs should be preserved in the parent namespace.
```suggestion
                # We normalize the namespace (dropping numeric segments and task IDs)
                # using `recast_checkpoint_ns` and then compute the parent namespace by
                # removing the last segment.
                recast_ns = recast_checkpoint_ns(ns)
                parent_ns = NS_SEP.join(recast_ns.split(NS_SEP)[:-1])
```

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Normalize cutoff format before SQLite string comparison**

`sweep_ttl` now binds an aware Python `datetime` directly, which SQLite adapts to strings like `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS+00:00`; however, `expires_at` is also written via `DATETIME(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, ...)` in `BaseSqliteStore._get_batch_GET_ops_queries` (no timezone suffix), so at an exact boundary (`expires_at == cutoff` at second precision) the lexical comparison still evaluates true (`'...00' < '...00+00:00'`) and rows are deleted even though the predicate is `<`. This introduces an off-by-boundary regression for deterministic sweeps when callers pass an explicit cutoff at whole-second UTC instants.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Apply cutoff normalization in async TTL sweep**

The async implementation has the same boundary bug as the sync one: binding an aware `datetime` cutoff (serialized with `+00:00`) is compared against `expires_at` values that may have been refreshed using `DATETIME(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, ...)` (no offset), so equality at second precision can be misclassified as expired under `<`. This makes `AsyncSqliteStore.sweep_ttl(now=...)` non-deterministic at the exact cutoff edge for refreshed TTL rows.

body:
**Security Issues**
- **Path Traversal / Arbitrary File Read via env file path (exfiltration risk)**
The deploy helper `_parse_env_from_config()` allows a project-controlled `langgraph.json` to specify an `env` path that is resolved and then read with `dotenv_values()` without verifying the path remains within the project root. A malicious repository can set `\"env\": \"../../.env\"` (or an absolute path like `\"/home/user/.env\"`) to cause the CLI to read arbitrary files on the user's machine. The parsed key/value pairs are then packaged into `secrets` and transmitted to the remote deployment API, enabling exfiltration of local secrets. This violates the repository's path traversal guardrails, which require `resolve()` plus `is_relative_to()` containment checks for local file paths.

**Recommendations**
- Restrict `env` file resolution to the project directory. After calling `.resolve()`, enforce `env_path.is_relative_to(config_path.parent)` (or equivalent) and reject absolute or out-of-tree paths with a clear error. Avoid reading files outside the project root.
author: corridor-security

body:
The `env` file path from `langgraph.json` is resolved and then read without verifying it remains within the project root. A malicious repository can set `\"env\"` to an absolute or traversed path (e.g., `../../.env` or `/home/user/.env`), causing the CLI to read arbitrary files on the user's machine. Parsed values are then sent as `secrets` to the remote service, enabling exfiltration of local secrets.

Vulnerable code:
```python
if isinstance(env_field, str):
    env_path = (config_path.parent / env_field).resolve()
else:
    env_path = pathlib.Path.cwd() / ".env"
return {k: v for k, v in dotenv_values(env_path).items() if v is not None}
```

This violates the project's path traversal guardrails, which require `.resolve()` and a containment check using `.is_relative_to()` against the expected directory.

Remediation: Validate that the resolved path stays under the project root and reject absolute/out-of-tree paths.

Example fix:
```python
env_path = (config_path.parent / env_field).resolve()
if not env_path.is_relative_to(config_path.parent):
    raise click.UsageError("The 'env' file path must reside within the project directory")
```


For more details, see the [finding in Corridor](https://app.corridor.dev/projects/310af3f2-00f7-413d-8311-2265c3518990/findings/d6502766-156d-4446-8613-5c6b1328fb20).

**Provide feedback**: Reply with whether this is a valid vulnerability or false positive to help improve Corridor's accuracy.

body:
**Security Issues**
- Insecure transport selection (cleartext HTTP) due to port-based scheme logic
Both the DNS-AID tool creation and resolver node select the HTTP/HTTPS scheme based solely on whether the port equals 443, ignoring the declared protocol from discovery. If an agent is published as HTTPS on a non-standard port (e.g., 8443), these functions will connect over HTTP in cleartext, exposing user queries and responses to interception or manipulation. This is a realistic risk when integrating third-party/discovered agents and can lead to sensitive data exposure.

Recommendations
- Derive the scheme from the discovered protocol (e.g., 'https' means HTTPS regardless of port), not the port number.
author: corridor-security

body:
The scheme is selected based on the port instead of the discovered protocol. This will use cleartext HTTP for any HTTPS agent not on port 443, exposing the query/response to interception.

```python
scheme = "https" if agent.port == 443 else "http"
base_url = f"{scheme}://{agent.endpoint}:{agent.port}"
```

Impact: If a discovered agent advertises protocol "https" on a non-standard port (e.g., 8443), the tool will connect using HTTP, potentially leaking sensitive data or enabling MITM attacks.

Remediation: Derive the scheme from the discovered protocol rather than port.

```suggestion
scheme = "https" if agent.protocol == "https" else "http"
```

For more details, see the [finding in Corridor](https://app.corridor.dev/projects/310af3f2-00f7-413d-8311-2265c3518990/findings/c89dbc54-147a-4f5f-9753-c9ae9db09aec).

**Provide feedback**: Reply with whether this is a valid vulnerability or false positive to help improve Corridor's accuracy.
author: corridor-security

body:
The resolver selects HTTP/HTTPS based solely on the port. This can downgrade HTTPS agents on non-standard ports to HTTP, causing cleartext transmission of queries and responses.

```python
protocol = agent.get("protocol", "https")
scheme = "https" if port == 443 else "http"
base_url = f"{scheme}://{host}:{port}"
```

Impact: Sensitive data sent to discovered agents may be exposed to interception if HTTPS is not honored when the port is not 443.

Remediation: Use the discovered protocol to determine the scheme, not the port.

```suggestion
scheme = "https" if protocol == "https" else "http"
```

For more details, see the [finding in Corridor](https://app.corridor.dev/projects/310af3f2-00f7-413d-8311-2265c3518990/findings/a6f93355-5313-456a-9120-775014fafe7d).

**Security Issues**
- **Arbitrary File Write via Unvalidated Config Path (Path Traversal/External Path Control)**  
The `_deploy` flow persists the deployment name into an environment file using a path derived from `langgraph.json` (`env` field) without constraining it to the project root. An attacker can craft a malicious repository with `langgraph.json` specifying an `env` path like `../../.bashrc` (or another existing file the user can write). When a user runs the CLI and is prompted for a deployment name, the code will write to that attacker-chosen file. This enables arbitrary file modification within the user's permissions and can be abused to corrupt files or influence shell startup files.

Recommendations:
- Canonicalize and enforce that the resolved env path remains within the expected project directory (e.g., `config_path.parent`) using `Path.resolve()` and `Path.is_relative_to()`.  
- Reject absolute paths and any path that escapes the project root.  
- Only write to a known-safe `.env` within the project when persisting values, or prompt the user explicitly before creating/writing to a path outside the project.
author: corridor-security

body:
Persisting the deployment name to a file path derived from `langgraph.json` without containment checks allows arbitrary file modification if a malicious repo sets `env` to an existing file outside the project (e.g., `../../.bashrc`).

```python
env_path = _resolve_env_path(config_json, config)
if env_path is not None:
    set_key(str(env_path), _DEPLOYMENT_NAME_ENV, name)
```

An attacker can craft a repo with a `langgraph.json` that sets `env` to an existing, writeable file outside the project. When a user runs the CLI and is prompted for a deployment name, `set_key()` will modify that file, leading to arbitrary file write within the user's privileges.

Remediation:
- Resolve the path and verify it remains within the project root using `Path.resolve()` and `Path.is_relative_to(config_path.parent)`. Reject absolute paths or any path escaping the project directory.
- Only allow writing to a `.env` file under the project root, or prompt the user before writing to any external file.

For more details, see the [finding in Corridor](https://app.corridor.dev/projects/310af3f2-00f7-413d-8311-2265c3518990/findings/4c18a7fa-614d-4dd2-8355-90babc3cb429).

**Security Issues**
- Command Injection in generated Dockerfile RUN commands
The Dockerfile generation embeds unquoted, user-influenced directory paths into shell commands (e.g., RUN cd {path} && ...). If a workspace/package directory contains spaces or shell metacharacters (e.g., ;, &&), this can break out of the cd argument and inject arbitrary shell commands during docker build. This is newly introduced in the uv_lock Dockerfile path as well as present in the modified node install path. 

Recommendations
- Quote all interpolated paths used in shell commands with shlex.quote() before embedding into RUN lines.
- Alternatively, use Dockerfile WORKDIR to change directories safely instead of shelling out with cd.
author: corridor-security

body:
Unquoted, user-influenced path is embedded into a shell command in the generated Dockerfile:

```python
f"RUN cd {local_deps.working_dir} && {_get_node_pm_install_cmd(config_path.parent)} && tsx /api/langgraph_api/js/build.mts",
```

If a workspace/package directory name contains spaces or shell metacharacters (e.g., `;`, `&&`), the `cd` argument can be truncated and the remainder treated as a separate command, enabling command injection at docker build time.

This pattern is also introduced for the uv/uv.lock workflow in `uv_lock.py` (the analogous `RUN cd {plan.working_dir} && ...` line) and should be fixed there as well.

CWE-78: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')

Remediation: Quote the directory path using `shlex.quote()` before embedding it into the `RUN` line, or use a Dockerfile `WORKDIR` step to avoid shell expansion.


For more details, see the [finding in Corridor](https://app.corridor.dev/projects/310af3f2-00f7-413d-8311-2265c3518990/findings/df5b8cdb-5797-4b84-9470-a6b04d328336).

body: The root `spell_check` target does not reliably fail the build when a library spell check fails. In a shell `for` loop, a failure in an earlier `$(MAKE) -C ...` can be overwritten by a later successful command, causing the overall target to exit 0 and letting CI miss typos. Make the loop fail-fast (e.g., `set -e; ...` or `|| exit $$?` after the sub-make) so any library failure propagates.
author: copilot-pull-request-reviewer

body: This existence check is based on the *success* of `make spell_check`, not whether the target exists. If `codespell` finds typos, `make spell_check` exits non-zero and the workflow will incorrectly print \"command not found\" and skip the step—masking real failures. Also, the step runs `make spell_check` twice. Prefer a non-executing check for the target (e.g., a dry-run) and then run `make spell_check` exactly once.

**Security Issues**
- **Command injection in Dockerfile generation (CWE-78, High):** In libs/cli/internal/config/docker.go, the Node Dockerfile generator embeds user-controlled CLI flags directly into RUN instructions without quoting/validation:
  - installStep = "RUN " + installCmd
  - buildStep = "RUN " + buildCommand
  These assignments (in the function that generates the Node Dockerfile; see the lines where installStep/buildStep are constructed in this file) allow injection of shell metacharacters (e.g., &&, ;, |), enabling arbitrary command execution during docker build. This violates project guardrail 2 (no unvalidated CLI-controlled commands in Dockerfile RUN) and poses a supply-chain risk (malicious commands executed in build context, poisoned images).
- **Sensitive token exposure via command-line arguments (CWE-522, CWE-200; High):** In runDeployMain (deployment flow), the registry push token is passed to docker login using the -p flag. Command-line arguments are visible to local users via process listings (ps, /proc) and may be captured by telemetry/logging, exposing the credential and enabling unauthorized pushes to the registry.

**Recommendations**
- **Harden Dockerfile command handling:**  
  - Prefer Dockerfile RUN exec form with validated/structured arguments (e.g., RUN ["npm","ci"] and RUN ["npm","run","build"]) instead of shell-form concatenation.  
  - If dynamic commands must be supported, strictly validate/whitelist allowable commands/subcommands and reject inputs containing shell metacharacters, newlines, or redirections.  
  - If quoting is unavoidable, use robust escaping and avoid invoking a shell (e.g., use exec form via go-containerregistry templating or JSON array serialization).  
  - Add unit tests and a guardrail check to prevent concatenating untrusted input into Dockerfile RUN lines in the future.
- **Protect the registry token in docker login:**  
  - Replace docker login -p <token> with docker login --password-stdin and pass the token via stdin using the subprocess StdinPipe API so it never appears in argv.  
  - Ensure no logs or error messages print the token; mask/redact sensitive values in debug output.  
  - Consider scoping the token to least privilege and short TTL to reduce blast radius if leaked.
author: corridor-security

body:
The deployment push token is passed to `docker login` via the `-p` flag, which exposes the credential in process arguments that can be read by other local users or tools.

Vulnerable code:
```go
_ = lgexec.Run("docker", []string{"login", "-u", "oauth2accesstoken", "-p", token, registryURL}, lgexec.RunOpts{})
```

Impact: Local users on the same system can obtain the token from process listings (e.g., `ps`, `/proc`), enabling unauthorized pushes to the registry.

Remediation: Use password-stdin to avoid placing secrets in argv.

Example fix:
```go
args := []string{"login", "-u", "oauth2accesstoken", "--password-stdin", registryURL}
if err := lgexec.Run("docker", args, lgexec.RunOpts{Stdin: strings.NewReader(token)}); err != nil {
    // handle error
}
```
Ensure the token is only passed via stdin and not logged or exposed elsewhere.

For more details, see the [finding in Corridor](https://app.corridor.dev/projects/310af3f2-00f7-413d-8311-2265c3518990/findings/c2818a97-9437-4154-b974-46d70ea110e7).

body:
**Security Issues**
- **Uncontrolled Resource Consumption (DoS) via unbounded pre-subscription buffering**  
  The new retain/buffering behavior introduced for EventLog and StreamMux child mini-muxes can retain all events before any subscriber attaches, with no size limits. In `StreamMux.make_child()`, every child mini-mux has `_events._retain = True` and all projection logs/channels also set to retain. If the caller never subscribes (e.g., never iterates `run.subgraphs` or their projections), these buffers will grow unbounded for the lifetime of the run. An attacker (or abusive user) can trigger long/large runs or deeply nested subgraphs to exhaust process memory, causing denial of service.  
  This is a regression from the prior "lazy-subscribe" semantics where pre-subscription pushes were dropped. The change applies broadly to all child mux projections (not only low-volume channels), significantly increasing DoS risk.

Recommendations
- Apply explicit upper bounds to retained buffers (e.g., configurable `maxlen`) and enforce them in EventLog and StreamChannel when `retain=True`.
- Limit retain to low-volume projections (e.g., lifecycle only), or retain only until the first subscription occurs.
- Consider conditional or time/window-bounded retention, and/or surface configuration to disable retain in sensitive deployments.
- Add safeguards to `make_child()` so that retain is not forced on all channels/logs, or guard by a bounded `maxlen` per projection.
author: corridor-security

body:
Unbounded pre-subscription buffering introduces a denial-of-service risk. Adding the `retain` flag and using it to bypass the pre-subscription no-op means EventLog can accumulate unbounded items before any consumer subscribes, with no `maxlen` enforced.

This enables memory exhaustion if an attacker or abusive user triggers long/large runs without ever subscribing to the projection (or to child subgraph handles).

Impacted code:
```python
def __init__(self, maxlen: int | None = None, *, retain: bool = False) -> None:
    ...
    # Pre-subscription pushes are silent no-ops unless `_retain` is True.
    self._subscribed = False
    self._retain = retain
...
def push(self, item: T) -> None:
    ...
    if not self._subscribed and not self._retain:
        return
```

Remediation: enforce a bounded capacity when `retain=True` (e.g., a default `maxlen`), or only retain a small window (time- or count-based). Alternatively, restrict `retain=True` to low-volume channels and automatically disable retention once a subscriber attaches.

For more details, see the [finding in Corridor](https://app.corridor.dev/projects/310af3f2-00f7-413d-8311-2265c3518990/findings/e24795bd-e199-4dae-9ff7-b94b5b16c709).

**Provide feedback**: Reply with whether this is a valid vulnerability or false positive to help improve Corridor's accuracy.
author: corridor-security

body:
Child mini-muxes force `retain=True` on all projection logs and channels, causing unbounded buffering if the caller never subscribes to `run.subgraphs` or the child projections. This significantly increases memory DoS risk for large/long runs or deep subgraph trees.

```python
def make_child(self, scope: tuple[str, ...]) -> StreamMux:
    ...
    child = StreamMux(...)
    # Retain pushes until consumer subscribes
    child._events._retain = True
    for value in child.extensions.values():
        if isinstance(value, EventLog):
            value._retain = True
        elif isinstance(value, StreamChannel):
            value._log._retain = True
```

Remediation: do not blanket-enable `retain` for all child projections. Restrict retention to low-volume channels (e.g., lifecycle) or enforce strict `maxlen` limits per projection. Consider disabling `retain` when the parent never subscribes to `subgraphs`, or only retaining a small bounded window until the first subscription.

body:
**Security Issues**
- **Race Condition via thread-local reentrancy guard used in async paths**  
The new reentrancy guard `_DELTA_RECONSTRUCTION = threading.local()` is used in both sync and async `get_channel_writes`/`aget_channel_writes`. In async servers, multiple concurrent requests typically execute on the same event loop thread; `threading.local()` is thread-local, not task-local. This allows one request (which sets `active=True`) to inadvertently affect another concurrent request on the same thread, causing the second to early-return empty writes. This cross-request interference can corrupt state reconstruction across tenants, leading to integrity issues or denial-of-service-like behavior (incomplete/incorrect state), which is exploitable by sending concurrent requests. Use `contextvars.ContextVar` or a scoped reentrancy guard that is task/request-local to avoid cross-request leakage.
author: corridor-security

body:
A thread-local reentrancy guard is used in both sync and async code paths, which is unsafe under asyncio because multiple concurrent requests on the same event loop thread will share the same `threading.local()` state. This can cause one request to suppress reconstruction for another, returning incomplete state across tenants (integrity issue/DoS). Use `contextvars.ContextVar` or a scoped per-call guard instead.

```python
# Global, thread-local (NOT task-local)
_DELTA_RECONSTRUCTION: threading.local = threading.local()
...
if getattr(_DELTA_RECONSTRUCTION, "active", False):
    return DeltaChannelWrites(writes=[])
...
_DELTA_RECONSTRUCTION.active = True
try:
    ...
finally:
    _DELTA_RECONSTRUCTION.active = False
```

Impact: In an async server where multiple requests run on the same thread, a concurrent call can set `active=True` and cause another user's `get_channel_writes()`/`aget_channel_writes()` to return empty writes, leading to incorrect or partial state reconstruction. This is a realistic cross-request race that can be triggered by an attacker via concurrency.

Remediation: Replace the thread-local flag with a task-local context using `contextvars.ContextVar`, or refactor the reentrancy guard to be per-invocation (e.g., pass a guard through the call chain) so concurrent requests cannot interfere with each other.

For more details, see the [finding in Corridor](https://app.corridor.dev/projects/310af3f2-00f7-413d-8311-2265c3518990/findings/d785ab01-6083-4950-bb65-41bd23883435).

**Provide feedback**: Reply with whether this is a valid vulnerability or false positive to help improve Corridor's accuracy.

body: `ToolRuntime` is part of the public `langgraph.prebuilt` API, and moving `tools` after `tool_call_id`/`store` changes the generated dataclass `__init__` parameter order. Any external callers using positional args (e.g., passing `tools` as the 5th argument) would now silently bind that value to `tool_call_id` instead. Consider preserving the previous parameter order by keeping `tools` in its original position and also giving `tool_call_id` and `store` defaults (so `tools` can use `default_factory` without reordering), or otherwise avoiding a positional-arg breaking change.

Changing the dataclass field order moves `tools` after `tool_call_id`/`store`, which changes the positional `ToolRuntime(...)` constructor signature for this public API (exported from `langgraph.prebuilt`). If external users instantiate `ToolRuntime` positionally, this becomes a breaking change. Consider keeping the original field order and instead giving later fields (`tool_call_id`, `store`, etc.) defaults (e.g., `None`) so `tools` can have a default without reordering, or otherwise explicitly document/guard against positional construction.
```suggestion
    tools: list[BaseTool] = field(default_factory=list)
    tool_call_id: str | None = None
    store: BaseStore | None = None
```

Casting JSON values to `double precision` and coercing the filter operand with `float(value)` can silently change large integers and high-precision decimals (for example values above `2^53`), so range filters may return the wrong rows near those boundaries. This regression is introduced by the new numeric path and affects any metadata using precise numeric IDs/counters; use `numeric` casting (and a non-float parameter type such as `Decimal`/string) to avoid precision loss.
